newsitem.title: USA: High gas prices fail to drive U.S utilities to oil.
newsitem.headline: High gas prices fail to drive U.S utilities to oil.

text.p: Utilities along the U.S. East Coast so far this autumn are sticking with natural gas for power generation despite rising gas prices and falling prices for rival heavy fuel oil, utility officials said.
"It's making fuel oil more attractive, but it's still not as attractive (as natural gas)," said an official at a New York utility.

East Coast utilities, claiming the nation's greatest concentration of duel-fuel power plants, typically switch between oil and gas whenever there is a sustained difference - at least a week - of a few cents per million British thermal units (mmBtu) at the burner tip.
"Utilities have great capability to switch to oil, but there are practical limitations," said Larry Goldstein, president of Petroleum Industry Research Associates.
Local taxes - about $3.00 for a barrel of heavy fuel oil in New York state - and environmental regulations may also discourage switching to oil during the winter, he said.

Gas prices in New York for November 1 delivery averaged 80 cents per mmBtu higher than on October 1. In Philadelphia, spot gas for next-day delivery soared to nearly $3.15/mmBtu, up sharply from $2.00 a month earlier.
While gas staged its seasonal rally, domestic fuel oil prices fell in line with easing crude oil prices worldwide.
In New York city, one percent sulphur residual fuel oil - the most common grade on the East Coast - was selling at about $19.60 a barrel, down more than a dollar from a month ago.
The region's utility demand for fuel oil typically begins to climb in November as spot gas supplies are increasingly diverted to meet residential customers' winter demands.

Oil merchants, citing high gas prices and the need to replace about 5,500 megawatts of electricity lost due to extended outages at several big regional nuclear power plants, have been predicting pent up fuel oil demand this winter.

While price is a key factor in deciding which fuel to buy for power generation, utility executives said other factors come into play, like projected daily demand, a plant's fuel efficiency, and the cost of starting up a fossil-fuel plant.
To offset higher gas costs this month, one Florida utility official said they were injecting high-sulphur fuel oil into the gas stream feeding burners at its dual-fuel power plants.
"It's not an 'either-or' situation with us," said one Virginia utility official.

Large oil-burning power plants offer far less flexibility in meeting power demand than smaller gas-fired units, he said, adding that combined-cycle plants are clearly more efficient and cheaper to run than oil units.
If electricity demand were to surge for only a few days, the utility would choose to start up a combined-cycle gas unit even if gas costs more than oil, he said.
But many utilities are finding that the cheapest way to cut power generating costs is to avoid buying either fuel.
"We're not burning oil or gas because it's cheaper to buy (power) in the open market," the New York utility official said.
